title: What If 90% of a Country's Women Stopped Working for a Day? Iceland Did It in 1975

scenes.text: What if 90 percent of a country's women stopped for a day? Iceland did. Sausages sold out.
October 24, 1975. Icelandic women earned about 40 percent less than men. So 90 percent took the day off: no paid work, no cooking, no childcare.
Banks closed. Factories stopped. Schools and nurseries shut. In a country of 220,000 people, 25,000 filled central Reykjavik.
Fathers had to take their children to the office, armed with sweets and coloring pencils. Easy-to-cook sausages vanished from the shelves.
Icelanders still call it the Long Friday. Five years later, Iceland elected Vigdis Finnbogadottir, the world's first democratically elected female president.
Today Iceland is the only country to have closed more than 90 percent of its gender gap. One day off. Never the same.

description:
What if 90 percent of a country's women stopped working for a day? On 24 October 1975, Iceland's Women's Day Off, about 90 percent of Icelandic women refused to do paid work, housework or childcare, at a time when women earned roughly 40 percent less than men.
Banks, factories, schools, nurseries and many shops closed, and about 25,000 people rallied in Reykjavik in a nation of around 220,000. Fathers took children to work and sausages sold out as the easiest meal to cook. In 1980 Iceland elected Vigdis Finnbogadottir, the world's first democratically elected female head of state, and the World Economic Forum now rates Iceland the only country to have closed more than 90 percent of its gender gap.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: Icelandic women repeated the strike in 1985, 2005, 2010, 2016, 2018 and 2023. What would stop if one group vanished for a day? Drop your own what-if below.
